newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FOCUS - Tietmeyer warns of insufficient convergence.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Tietmeyer warns of insufficient convergence.

text.p: Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer, without referring directly to the European Union's planned single currency. warned on Friday that fixed exchange rates between nations lacking sufficient convergence would be both dangerous and counterproductive.
The German central bank chief said "fixed exchange rates with insufficient convergence would be dangerous and counterproductive".

A system that joined nations that lacked the necessary economic convergence would sooner or later lead to conflict between those nations and would not stand up to the test of unforgiving financial markets in the long term, he said.
Taking apparent pains to avoid mention of the European economic and monetary union (UMU) due to start in 1999, Tietmeyer spoke in global terms.

Speaking at a Czech-German Chamber of Commerce meeting in Prague, he said that in today's multi-faceted world of large industrial nations and regions, the necessary political and economic convergence would prove difficult to achieve or maintain.

"Cooperation always becomes difficult when it needs to pull all nations into one boat," he said. "We already see how difficult it is to make tax systems compatible, let alone harmonise them, within the European Union."

On the planned euro single currency, Tietmeyer said: "It cannot be ruled out that in a case of extreme political differences, for example between Europe and the United States, that there could be certain phases of greater (international exchange rate) fluctuation."
On the other hand, Tietmeyer added that a sustainable and stable euro would without doubt bring benefits, such as lower interest rates and improved competition.

The Bundesbank president warned, however, that the euro could not automatically lead to Europe's economic success, stressing that such success depended largely on how willing and able nations were to deal with their structural problems.
The German central bank, seen as Europe's most uncompromising defender of currency stability, was formulating its policy with the best interests of the euro in mind, Tietmeyer said.

"This is what the Bundesbank is working for -- not because we have a fetish for stability, but out of our reponsibility for a permanently competitive, prosperous and at the same time conflict-free Europe," he said.
